analysis.one_liner: Requires warehouse employers to disclose quotas, limit quota tracking, guarantee paid breaks, and set ergonomic safety standards.
analysis.headline: The Warehouse Worker Protection Act was introduced in May 2024 with 10 cosponsors, never received a committee vote or Senate floor action, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first federal rules for warehouse work quotas. Employers in warehousing, wholesale, and package delivery would have had to tell workers in writing what quota they face, how speed data and surveillance track them, and what discipline can follow a miss. It would have banned quotas that cut into bathroom breaks or legally required rest, barred disciplining workers over unannounced or ranking-only quotas, guaranteed a paid 15-minute break every four hours, and directed OSHA to write ergonomic and injury-treatment standards for warehouses. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and fulfillment center workers subject to productivity quotas, including many at large e-commerce and package-delivery operations. The bill defines quotas broadly to cover not just explicit targets but implied ones, speed tracking, and time-tallied monitoring, so the disclosure, data-access, and anti-discipline rules would reach workers who are pushed by quotas without ever being handed a written number. It also protects contract, temp, and staffing-agency workers doing warehouse work, and requires notices in English, Spanish, and each worker's primary language.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Warehouse and fulfillment workers under quotas

how_it_helps.text: Each covered employer must give workers a written description of every quota they face: the number or speed required, how targets are calculated, the discipline a miss can bring, and exactly what work-speed data and surveillance technology is collecting on them [S2].

Employers cannot impose quotas that interfere with legally required meal and rest breaks, bathroom use including travel time, safety rules, or anti-discrimination rights, and cannot measure workers' output during breaks [S2].

A worker cannot be disciplined for missing a quota that was never disclosed, that is based solely on ranking against other workers, or that is built on continuous second-by-second monitoring, and employers must hand over a human-readable copy of the speed data behind any adverse action [S2].

Workers, union representatives, and worker advocacy groups get a right to request an individual's work-speed data and the aggregated data for comparable workers at the same site, at no cost, up to three years after a job ends [S2].
Every four hours of work comes with a guaranteed paid 15-minute rest break, plus posted and take-home notice of that right and of the ban on retaliation for using it [S2].

Retaliation gets a rebuttable presumption: any adverse action within 90 days of a worker exercising these rights is presumed unlawful unless the employer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence [S2].

Claims under the bill cannot be forced into pre-dispute arbitration, class-action hurdles are relaxed, and labor violations carry civil penalties up to $76,987 per violation and $769,870 for repeat or willful ones [S2].

OSHA must issue ergonomic standards for warehouse musculoskeletal-injury hazards within 4 years and standards requiring trained first-aiders and prompt medical referral on site within 3 years, and employers must start fixing serious, willful, or repeated safety violations while they contest them [S2].

The Labor Department must open an investigation, including an on-site inspection, within 30 days at any large warehouse employer with an injury rate at least 1.5 times the warehousing-industry average, or after 5 credible complaints in a year [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse operators, e-commerce fulfillment companies, wholesalers, and package carriers would bear the costs: writing and updating quota disclosures, limiting or restructuring speed tracking and surveillance software, paying new mandated breaks, keeping and sharing work-speed records, paying up to roughly $77,000 per violation (and nearly $770,000 for repeat or willful ones), and funding on-site occupational medicine consultation under the OSHA standards. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers through prices, and companies currently using ranking-based or continuously monitored quota systems would have to change how they manage and discipline workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large warehouse operators and e-commerce companies

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost and operational disruption: quota systems keep fulfillment fast and inexpensive, and the bill would force large operators to redesign how they set targets, monitor workers, and handle discipline, with some of that cost likely passed to consumers in the form of slower deliveries or higher prices [S2].

The bill is broad and prescriptive: it reaches not just warehousing but wholesale distribution, electronic shopping and mail-order, and courier operations, and it dictates specific break intervals, data formats, notice timelines (some as short as 2 business days), and statutory penalty amounts rather than leaving those to regulators [S2].

Its protections only apply to workers who are subject to a quota as the bill defines it, so warehouse workers at facilities without defined performance standards would get the paid-break guarantee but not the quota-disclosure and data-access rights [S2].
As an authorization of appropriations for whatever sums are necessary, its enforcement staff, advisory board, and inspections would depend entirely on future funding decisions by Congress [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in five American workers in warehousing and fulfillment who work under algorithmic quotas, the bill offered concrete, verifiable rights: knowing the number, seeing the data used against you, and being able to dispute it. The real costs fall on a small set of large, highly profitable logistics and e-commerce firms, and some would reach consumers as modest price or speed changes. The main design weakness is the same breadth that gives it force: it writes detailed operational rules into statute for a fast-changing industry, and enforcement depends on appropriations that never would have been guaranteed. On balance the trade is strongly one-sided in favor of workers, which is exactly why the industry side of the ledger never got a hearing in the committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill in the Senate on May 2, 2024, joined on introduction by Sens. Casey, Smith, and Brown [S4][S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
That referral is the last entry in the bill's full action history; the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S4].
Ten senators cosponsored the bill: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents [S3].
No Republican cosponsored, and the bill's congressional page shows no further action before the 118th Congress ended [S1][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large warehouse, e-commerce fulfillment, wholesale distribution, and package-delivery companies are better off because the bill never moved: they avoided quota disclosure, surveillance limits, mandated paid breaks, data-access rights, new civil penalties of up to $76,987 per violation, and OSHA ergonomics and injury-treatment standards for warehouse work. Warehouse workers under quotas get no federal protections from this bill, though some states have since moved on their own.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter was a Democrat or Independent — 9 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 4 Independents, led by Sen. Markey — and no Republican cosponsored or voted on the bill at any stage.

industries.industry: Warehousing, e-commerce fulfillment, and package delivery (Amazon, UPS, FedEx and peers)
industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on these operators: quota disclosure, surveillance limits, mandated paid breaks, data access for workers and unions, penalties up to $769,870 for repeat willful violations, and new OSHA ergonomics and medical-treatment standards. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs against the workers the bill protects.

Covered facilities include merchant wholesalers under NAICS codes 423 and 424, so wholesalers with quota systems would face the same disclosure, break, and recordkeeping duties as e-commerce warehouses.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and temp-worker firms serving warehouses
industries.note: They are covered employers under the bill, so they must comply, but their temp workers also gain the same quota-disclosure, break, and anti-retaliation rights as direct hires, closing a common gap in workplace protections.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and workforce-management technology vendors
industries.note: The bill restricts collection to what is strictly necessary for quota monitoring, requires disclosure of the vendor's identity and data transfers, and bans discipline based on continuous time-tallying — shrinking the market for second-by-second worker-monitoring tools.
